terms.meaning: Sound that the listener does not want.
terms.example: A film song you love is music at a wedding. The same song, played loudly next door at midnight, is noise to you.
terms.art: A child with a pillow over her head while a speaker plays across the street.

terms.meaning: A very fast shaking to and fro.
terms.example: Touch a steel plate while a mixer-grinder is running. The shaking you feel is vibration.
terms.art: A hand resting on a humming steel plate.

terms.meaning: A moving pattern of air that is squeezed and then stretched, which carries sound from its source to your ear.
terms.example: Clap once. The air is pushed outward in a sound wave that reaches the wall and your ear.
terms.art: A hand clap with rings of squeezed and stretched air spreading out from it.

terms.meaning: A message carried by something that changes, such as a sound, a light or a nerve's tiny electric pulse.
terms.example: A pressure cooker's whistle is a signal that the steam inside is ready.
terms.art: A pressure cooker with a whistle and small wavy lines leaving it.

terms.meaning: Something put into the air, water or soil that can harm the beings who share it.
terms.example: Smoke from a bonfire is a pollutant of the air. Indian law also counts loud noise as one.
terms.art: A chimney with smoke on one side and a loudspeaker with sound lines on the other.

terms.meaning: The unit for how strong a sound is. It is written dB.
terms.example: Whispering is about 30 decibels. Ordinary talking is about 60. A mixer-grinder at arm's length is about 90.
terms.art: A ladder of sounds from a whisper to a mixer-grinder, each with its decibel number.

terms.meaning: The energy a sound carries as it moves through the air.
terms.example: A loud horn carries far more sound energy to your ear in each second than a whisper does.
terms.art: A whisper and a horn drawn with small and large piles of energy blocks.

terms.meaning: A tool with a microphone and a display that shows how strong a sound is, in decibels.
terms.example: A teacher holds a sound-level meter at the back of the hall to check the band is not too loud.
terms.art: A hand-held meter with a small screen showing 72.

terms.meaning: How high or low a sound is.
terms.example: A mosquito's whine has a high pitch. A truck's rumble has a low pitch.
terms.art: A mosquito with a thin high line and a truck with a thick low line.

terms.meaning: A way of measuring sound so that each pitch counts about as much as a human ear hears it. It is written dB(A).
terms.example: India's noise limits are given in dB(A), because they are meant to protect human ears.
terms.art: A graph showing that human ears hear middle pitches best and very low rumbles poorly.

terms.meaning: A small part that turns the shaking of sound into a tiny electric signal.
terms.example: The tiny hole at the bottom of your phone is the opening to its microphone.
terms.art: A phone with an arrow pointing at the microphone hole.

terms.meaning: The middle value of a measurement that keeps jumping up and down, taken over a set time.
terms.example: A meter jumps between 55 and 75 on a street. Over 30 seconds the average reading may be 66.
terms.art: A meter display with a jumping number and a steady average number beside it.

terms.meaning: The coiled, liquid-filled part of the inner ear where vibration becomes nerve signals. It is about the size of a pea.
terms.example: Your cochlea is curled like a tiny snail shell, deep inside the bone beside each ear.
terms.art: A cut-open snail-shaped tube with a zoom circle.

terms.meaning: A sensing cell in the cochlea with a tuft of tiny stiff hairs. When the tuft bends, the cell sends a signal.
terms.example: A loud night of crackers can bend the hair cells so far that some do not recover.
terms.art: A hair cell with an upright tuft and a nerve below it.

terms.meaning: A tiny electric pulse that travels along a nerve to carry a message to the brain.
terms.example: When a hair cell bends, a nerve signal runs to your brain and you hear a sound.
terms.art: A line of small pulses running along a nerve towards a brain.

terms.meaning: The unit for how many vibrations happen in one second. It is written Hz.
terms.example: A note of 4,000 hertz is a very high whistle. The air shakes 4,000 times each second.
terms.art: A string vibrating with a counter that reads 4,000 each second.

terms.meaning: To grow back after being lost or damaged.
terms.example: A lizard can regrow her tail. A bird can regrow the hair cells in her ear. A person cannot.
terms.art: A lizard with a new tail and a bird with new hair cells.

terms.meaning: A small device worn in or behind the ear that makes sounds louder.
terms.example: A grandfather with a hearing aid can follow the talk at the dinner table again.
terms.art: An older man with a small device behind his ear.

terms.meaning: A device placed inside the ear in an operation. It sends electrical signals straight to the hearing nerve.
terms.example: A child may receive a cochlear implant when her hair cells cannot send signals.
terms.art: A cut-away ear showing a thin wire inside the cochlea.

terms.meaning: A word, written with a capital D, for people who do not hear much or at all and who often belong to a community that signs.
terms.example: Many Deaf people in India use Indian Sign Language and see it as a full language of their own.
terms.art: Two children signing to each other across a table.

terms.meaning: A full language made with the hands, face and body, with its own grammar.
terms.example: Indian Sign Language has signs for words, and a person can tell a story in it, just as in Tamil or Hindi.
terms.art: Two hands making a sign with a smiling face.

terms.meaning: Dull and hard to hear, as if wrapped in cotton.
terms.example: After a loud wedding band, the world may sound muffled for some hours.
terms.art: A child with a cotton-wool cloud around her head.

terms.meaning: A ringing, buzzing or hissing heard in the ear when no sound is outside.
terms.example: After a loud function, a boy hears a thin ringing in bed at night. That is tinnitus.
terms.art: A head with a thin wavy line inside one ear.

terms.meaning: The idea that loud sound can destroy links between hair cells and the nerve, though a normal hearing test still passes.
terms.example: A person passes a hearing test, yet cannot follow talk in a noisy crowd.
terms.art: A hair cell joined to a nerve by links, half of them missing.

terms.meaning: A link that joins one cell to another so a signal can pass.
terms.example: The connections between a hair cell and its nerve carry each sound towards the brain.
terms.art: Two cells joined by a small bridge.

terms.meaning: The ear's automatic tightening of a tiny muscle when a loud sound arrives. It lowers the sound that reaches the inner ear.
terms.example: When a loud lorry passes, your acoustic reflex tightens in about a tenth of a second.
terms.art: A tiny muscle pulling on a small ear bone.

terms.meaning: The thin skin stretched across the inside of the ear, which shakes when sound reaches it.
terms.example: A sound enters your ear and shakes your eardrum, like the skin of a drum.
terms.art: A thin skin across a tube with sound lines hitting it.

terms.meaning: The air-filled space behind the eardrum that holds three tiny bones.
terms.example: Vibration from the eardrum crosses the middle ear along three tiny bones.
terms.art: Three tiny linked bones inside a small cavity.

terms.meaning: A sound that rises to full strength almost at once and is over in a moment.
terms.example: A burst balloon, a cap gun and a cracker all make a bang.
terms.art: A burst balloon with a sharp spiky sound line.

terms.meaning: The scientists' name for a bang: one very short, very sharp jump in air pressure.
terms.example: A cracker makes an impulse sound, which is why its loudness is measured in a special way.
terms.art: A tall thin spike on a sound graph.

terms.meaning: India's rule that a cracker must not make more than 125 decibels measured 4 metres from where it bursts.
terms.example: A cracker sold in a shop must stay under the firecracker limit, but a child holding one stands much closer than 4 metres.
terms.art: A cracker with a mark 4 metres away and a child standing at 1 metre.

terms.meaning: The body's alarm reaction, with faster heartbeat and tense muscles, when something seems like danger.
terms.example: A sudden horn makes your heart beat faster. That is the body's stress reaction.
terms.art: A child jumping at a horn with a heart drawn racing.

terms.meaning: How hard the blood pushes against the insides of the blood tubes.
terms.example: When you are startled, your blood pressure goes up for a short time.
terms.art: A blood tube with arrows pushing outward.

terms.meaning: Unwanted or harmful sound that is put into the shared air.
terms.example: Constant horns on a street are noise pollution for everyone and everything that lives beside it.
terms.art: A street with horn sound lines filling the air above the houses.

terms.meaning: A part of a town where people live in houses and flats.
terms.example: A lane of homes, a small temple and a corner tea shop is a residential area.
terms.art: A quiet lane of homes with a small tea shop.

terms.meaning: The area within 100 metres of a hospital, a school or a court, where India's rules set the strictest noise limits.
terms.example: A 'No Horn' board on a road beside a hospital marks a silence zone.
terms.art: A hospital with a ring around it and a 'No Horn' board.

terms.meaning: A device that turns an electric signal back into sound, often to reach many people.
terms.example: A loudspeaker on a pole carries a festival song across the whole neighbourhood.
terms.art: A pole with two horn-shaped loudspeakers and sound lines fanning out.

terms.meaning: The place where a sound begins.
terms.example: The source of a bus horn is the horn. The source of your voice is your throat.
terms.art: A horn with sound lines leaving it.

terms.meaning: Something placed in the path of sound that blocks or reduces it.
terms.example: A thick wall between a road and a school is a barrier to traffic sound.
terms.art: A wall between a loud road and a house.

terms.meaning: The total amount of something a body takes in. For sound, it depends on how loud it is and for how long.
terms.example: A loud sound for a short while and a quieter sound for much longer can give the same dose to the ear.
terms.art: A tap filling a glass, with loudness as the tap's width and time as how long it runs.

terms.meaning: A small soft plug that fits in the ear canal and lowers the sound that reaches the ear.
terms.example: A drummer pushes foam earplugs gently into her ears before practice.
terms.art: A pair of foam earplugs beside an ear.

terms.meaning: A pair of cups that cover the whole ear and lower the sound that reaches it.
terms.example: A road-drill worker wears ear muffs over both ears.
terms.art: A person in ear muffs beside a drill.

terms.meaning: A small speaker worn in or on the ear, which puts sound straight into the ear canal.
terms.example: A boy listens to songs through earphones on the bus.
terms.art: A child wearing earphones with a volume bar.

terms.meaning: The total amount of listening an ear can safely take in one week.
terms.example: For a child, the World Health Organization's weekly allowance is 75 decibels for up to 40 hours.
terms.art: A weekly calendar with listening hours shaded in.

terms.meaning: To soak sound up so that little of it bounces back.
terms.example: A thick curtain absorbs sound, so a room with curtains sounds softer.
terms.art: A soft curtain with sound lines fading into it.

terms.meaning: To bounce back from a surface.
terms.example: A bare wall reflects sound, so a shout in an empty room comes back to you.
terms.art: A sound line bouncing off a hard wall.

terms.meaning: To remove each other when two opposite things are added together.
terms.example: Two waves that squeeze and stretch the air in exactly opposite ways cancel each other and leave a flat line.
terms.art: Two opposite waves adding up to a flat line.

terms.meaning: Using a speaker to play the opposite of an incoming sound so the two cancel.
terms.example: Noise-cancelling headphones quieten the steady drone of an aeroplane engine.
terms.art: A pair of headphones with two opposite waves meeting inside.

terms.meaning: A part that lets air or gas pass through but makes the sound bounce around inside until it fades. It is also called a baffle.
terms.example: The silencer under a scooter is a metal box that makes the engine's bang much quieter.
terms.art: A cut-open metal box with chambers and holes, and wavy lines fading inside it.

terms.meaning: A signal made to tell you that danger is near, so you can act.
terms.example: The shrill beep of a smoke alarm is a warning to wake up and leave.
terms.art: A smoke alarm with sharp sound lines above a bed.

terms.meaning: A loud warning sound that usually rises and falls in pitch.
terms.example: An ambulance siren tells the traffic ahead to move aside.
terms.art: An ambulance with sweeping sound lines.

terms.meaning: To find where something is.
terms.example: With two ears you can locate a ringing bell, even with your eyes shut.
terms.art: A child with closed eyes pointing towards a ringing bell.

terms.meaning: A sound an animal makes when she or he senses danger, which warns others.
terms.example: A langur's bark is an alarm call that makes chital deer run.
terms.art: A langur barking on a branch above deer.

terms.meaning: Playing a recorded sound to animals to see how they respond.
terms.example: Scientists hid a loudspeaker in the grass and played back a leopard alarm call to vervet monkeys.
terms.art: A hidden loudspeaker in grass with monkeys looking towards it.

terms.meaning: Becoming so used to frequent warnings that you stop responding to them.
terms.example: A nurse who hears hundreds of beeps a shift may stop noticing a real one. That is alarm fatigue.
terms.art: A nurse surrounded by many small beeping symbols.

terms.meaning: Having no sound at all. Nobody who can hear has ever found it fully.
terms.example: A very quiet room still has your breath, your blood and the faint hiss of your own ears. So full silence is hard to find.
terms.art: A person in a foam-lined room with two small sound lines inside the body.

terms.meaning: A sound that bounces back from a hard surface so that you hear it again.
terms.example: If you shout in a stairwell with bare walls, you hear your own voice come back.
terms.art: A child shouting in a stairwell with a returning sound line.

experiments.title: A noise map of my home and street: which places are loudest, and are they within the limit?
experiments.question: How loud is each place in and around your home, and which of them are above India's limit for homes?
experiments.predict: Before you measure each place, write a guess in decibels and say why you think so. Is the kitchen with the mixer-grinder louder than the street? Is the bedroom window quieter when it is shut?
experiments.fair_test: Only the place or the time changes. The same phone is held the same way each time: at arm's length, at chest height, with the microphone end towards the sound. Each reading is the average over 30 seconds, taken twice. If the two readings differ by more than 5 decibels, a passing horn probably spoiled one, so take a third and use the middle one. For the distance readings, the sound source, its volume and the room stay the same, and only your distance changes.
results_table: How much I wanted this sound (1 to 5)
Backup: steps away I can still hear a ticking clock

materials.item: a phone with a free sound-meter app that shows an average reading
a second phone, a radio or a small speaker to play a steady sound at the ordinary volume of a talking voice
a mixer-grinder, run by a grown-up for 30 seconds with a little water inside
a ticking clock or a wristwatch, only for the no-app backup
paper, a pencil and a clock or phone timer
chalk or strips of paper tape, to mark 1, 2 and 4 big steps from the sound

experiments.safety: Make no loud sound near anyone's ears for this test. Keep the played sound at the volume of ordinary talk, and never use crackers or horns. A grown-up runs the mixer-grinder and takes the late-night reading.

schedule.what: Set up the meter, write all eight guesses, then measure the bedroom, the kitchen, the distance steps and the street by day.
At about a quarter past ten at night, a grown-up takes the street reading from the same spot, and you finish the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all eight readings. Draw a rough map of your home and street, and write each middle reading on the place where you took it. Colour the street readings above India's limit for homes red. Then write one sentence each for what you think, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this investigation you use a phone as a sound meter and measure eight places and times in and around your home. You find out which places are loud, how fast sound fades with distance, and how your readings compare with India's limits.

setup.art: A child holding a phone at arm's length at chest height with the microphone end pointing at a window, a watch showing 30 seconds.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the phone at arm's length, at chest height. Read the average over 30 seconds.

setup.art: A paper table with eight rows for places and a guess column already filled in with pencil numbers.
setup.caption: 2. Write your guess for every place before you measure any of them.

setup.art: A small speaker on a table and three chalk marks on the floor at 1, 2 and 4 big steps, with the child standing at the second mark holding the phone.
setup.caption: 3. Play a steady sound and measure at 1, 2 and 4 big steps away.

setup.art: A child at a window with the phone held out and the street below, beside a hand-drawn map with numbers written in colour.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the street from the window, by day and again late at night, and write the numbers on your map.

flow.do: Pick a free sound-meter app and open it. Hold the phone at arm's length, at chest height, with the microphone end (the bottom edge on most phones) towards the sound. Practise in the room where you are. Watch the number for 30 seconds on a timer and write the average if the app shows one. If it shows only a jumping number, write the number it shows most often.
flow.say: A sound meter turns the shaking of air into a number of decibels. Hold the phone out, away from your body, and watch it for half a minute. What do you see the number do?
flow.kid: Hold the phone out at arm's length. Watch the number for 30 seconds. Write the average.
flow.parent: Phone apps can differ from one another by several decibels, so this test compares one place with another. It does not prove that a law was broken. If you cannot get an app, use the backup. In every place, count the big steps you can walk away from a ticking clock while still hearing it. Write the number in the last column of the table. Examples of apps are the NIOSH Sound Level Meter on iPhone, or any free decibel app on Android. The farther you can hear it, the quieter the place.

flow.do: Draw the table with eight rows. Make rows for the bedroom with the window shut and open, and for the kitchen with the mixer-grinder running. Add rows for the street side by day and after 10 at night. Add three rows for the steady sound at 1, 2 and 4 big steps. Write a guess in decibels for every row now, before measuring anything, and a few words on why. Use these for help: a whisper is about 30, ordinary talk about 60 and a mixer-grinder at arm's length about 90.
flow.say: Before we measure, what do you think each number will be? Write a guess for every row and tell me why you think so. We will not change them later, even if they are wrong.
flow.kid: Write a guess for every row. Do not change them later.

ask.q: Which place do you think will be the loudest, and which the quietest?
good: Any answer with a reason, such as the kitchen loudest because the mixer-grinder is loud, and the closed bedroom quietest.
An answer that gives a reason about walls, windows or distance.

flow.parent: Wrong guesses are the useful part of this test. Do not correct the child. Let the meter do that.

flow.do: Measure the bedroom with the window shut and then open. Stand in the middle of the room, hold the phone as before, and read the 30-second average twice for each. Then ask a grown-up to run the mixer-grinder for 30 seconds with a little water inside. Stand one big step away and read the average once, and then a second time with another 30 seconds of grinding. Write all the numbers.
flow.say: Stay still and quiet for the whole 30 seconds, because your own voice and footsteps count too. Is the open window louder than the shut one? By how much?
flow.kid: Measure the bedroom with the window shut and open. Then measure the kitchen while the mixer-grinder runs. Write each number.

ask.q: What changed when the window was opened, and what does that tell you about where the sound comes from?
good: The number went up, so a lot of the sound comes in from outside.
A glass window and walls block some sound, and an open window lets it in.

flow.parent: A grown-up runs the mixer-grinder and keeps it to 30 seconds twice. Tell the child before it starts, and let them cover their ears if they wish. Keep the child at the one-step mark and not close to the jar. Two runs of 30 seconds at one big step away are fine for the ears. Do not run it for much longer than a minute or two in all.

flow.do: Play a steady sound on the second phone, radio or speaker, at the volume of ordinary talk. Put it on a table. Mark 1, 2 and 4 big steps from it with chalk or paper tape. Read the 30-second average at each mark, twice each. Do not raise the volume between marks. If the reading at 1 step is above about 70 decibels, turn the volume down and start again.
flow.say: The sound stays the same. Only you move. What do you think happens to the number each time you double the distance?
flow.kid: Stand at 1, 2 and 4 big steps from the sound. Read the number at each.

ask.q: How much did the number change each time you doubled your distance?
good: It fell by a few decibels each time, about 3 to 6.
It fell by about the same amount each doubling, so the drop was steady.

flow.parent: Outdoors in an open space, each doubling of distance lowers the level by about 6 decibels. In a room, walls bounce the sound back, so you will usually see a smaller drop, often 3 to 5. Both are normal. Two phones in the same place may disagree by a few decibels. The drop each time you move should still look alike.

flow.do: Go to a window, a balcony or the gate where the street can be heard. Stay with a grown-up. Read the 30-second average twice, in daytime, and write the numbers. If a horn or a bus passes, take a third reading and keep the middle one.
flow.say: This is the street at its busiest. Listen first. Which sounds do you want to hear, and which would you switch off if you could?
flow.kid: Stand at the window with a grown-up. Read the street's number twice.

ask.q: Which sounds were in the street reading, and which were you glad to hear?
good: Any honest list, such as horns, a vendor's call, a crow or a bell, with some marked wanted and some unwanted.
An answer that notices the meter counts all of them the same.

flow.parent: Stay at a window or gate and do not go near the road. If your home is near a hospital, school or court, tell the child that this place may be a silence zone, with the lowest limits.

flow.do: Write India's limits for homes in the table. A residential area is allowed 55 decibels by day and 45 at night, measured outside. A silence zone is allowed 50 and 40. The rules measure outside homes, so colour only the street readings that are above the limit red. Then give each of the eight sounds a mark from 1 to 5 for how much you wanted it. Compare the order of the decibel numbers with the order of your marks.
flow.say: Which street readings are above the limit? Now look at your wanting marks. Is the loudest place also the one you most wanted to be quiet?
flow.kid: Colour the street readings above the limit red. Mark each sound from 1 to 5 for how much you wanted it.

ask.q: Does the order of the numbers match the order of how much you wanted each sound?
good: Not always. A sound can be loud and wanted, or quiet and unwanted.
An answer that says the meter measures strength and cannot measure wanting.

flow.parent: The rules measure outside homes, so only the street readings can be compared with them. The other places are for comparing one place with another. Day means 6 in the morning to 10 at night.
flow.think: The meter can say how strong a sound is. Who can say whether it is noise?

flow.do: At about a quarter past ten at night, or any time after 10, a grown-up goes to the same window. They take two 30-second readings from the same place. Write them in the table. Compare the night number with the day number and with the night limit of 45 for homes. Then draw your map of your home and street, with each middle reading written on its place.
flow.say: The street at night is not the same street. Is it quieter? Is it quiet enough?
flow.kid: A grown-up takes the night reading. Then draw the map and write the numbers on it.
flow.parent: If the child is asleep, take the reading yourself and tell the story in the morning. Write what you could hear, such as a lorry, a dog or a distant loudspeaker. If the reading is above 45, remember that it is one reading from one phone, so it is a pointer and not proof.

experiments.title: Which cuts a steady sound the most: more distance, a quieter source or a barrier?
experiments.question: The three ways to protect the ear are a quieter source, more distance or a barrier, and less time. Which of the first two cuts a steady sound the most, and which material makes the best barrier?
experiments.predict: Guess which will lower the reading most. Will it be doubling the distance, turning the volume down by three clicks, or standing a pile of books between the speaker and the phone? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: The same steady sound plays at the same volume from the same place, and the measuring phone stays at the same height and angle. For each test only one thing changes: the distance, the volume or the barrier. Each reading is the 30-second average, taken twice, and the middle value is used because one passing horn can spoil a reading.

materials.item: a phone with a free sound-meter app
a second phone, a radio or a small speaker to play a steady sound
a sheet of paper stood up on its edge, taped to a book
a wall of 6 to 8 hardback books or full school bags, about 30 centimetres tall and 40 centimetres wide
a thick folded blanket or quilt, held upright by a chair
a tape measure, or a string with a knot every 50 centimetres
a quiet room with the door shut and the fan off

experiments.safety: Keep the sound at the volume of ordinary talk. Do not play anything loud near anyone's ears.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Work out the drop in each row by taking the middle reading from the starting reading. Put the changes in order from the biggest drop to the smallest. Then write one sentence each for what you think, what you saw and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment you test three ways of lowering a steady sound at one listening place. They are more distance, a quieter source and three kinds of barrier. You find out which lever works best, and why it matters for protecting ears.

setup.art: A small speaker on a table in a quiet room, a phone on a stack of books 50 centimetres away facing it, and a tape measure along the table.
setup.caption: 1. Put the speaker at one end of a table and the phone 50 centimetres away. Read the starting level.

setup.art: The same table with the phone moved to 1 metre, and a second picture with the speaker volume bar three clicks lower.
setup.caption: 2. Move the phone to 100 centimetres. Then put it back and turn the speaker down three clicks.

setup.art: Three barriers in turn between the speaker and the phone: a standing sheet of paper, a wall of books and a folded blanket.
setup.caption: 3. Put each barrier between the speaker and the phone, close to the speaker.

setup.art: A paper table with the rows filled in and a bar chart beside it, showing the longest bar for the biggest drop.
setup.caption: 4. Work out each drop and draw one bar for each change.

flow.do: Put the speaker at one end of a table, playing a steady sound at the volume of ordinary talk. A song with an even beat, or a recording of a fan, will do. Place the measuring phone 50 centimetres away, at the same height, with its microphone end towards the speaker. Read the 30-second average twice. This is the starting reading.
flow.say: We have one steady sound and one listening place. Write your guess first. Which of the three changes will cut the sound the most?
flow.kid: Play a steady sound. Read the level 50 centimetres away. Write it.

ask.q: Which change do you think will cut the sound the most, and why?
good: Any guess with a reason, such as the barrier because it stands in the way, or the distance because the sound spreads out.
An answer that thinks about sound spreading or being blocked.

flow.parent: Do not move the speaker or the phone angle again. If the readings jump about by more than 5 decibels, close the door, switch off the fan and try again. If you have no meter app, use the backup. Stand where you can just hear a ticking clock. Count the big steps you can walk back, with and without each barrier.

flow.do: Move the phone to 100 centimetres from the speaker, which is double the distance. Read the average twice and write it. Move the phone back to 50 centimetres. Then turn the speaker's volume down by three clicks on the volume button, and read twice again at 50 centimetres. Put the volume back up.
flow.say: Distance first, then quieter volume. How much did each one change the number?
flow.kid: Double the distance. Read. Then go back and turn the volume down three clicks. Read.

ask.q: Which gave the bigger drop, double the distance or three clicks lower?
good: The answer from the table, with the two numbers.
A guess about why, such as that the sound spreads out as it travels.

flow.parent: In a room, doubling the distance usually lowers the level by 3 to 6 decibels. Three volume clicks lowers it by a very different amount depending on the phone, so there is no right number. Both are results, not mistakes.

flow.do: Tape the sheet of paper to a book so that it stands upright on its edge. Put it between the speaker and the phone, close to the speaker. Read twice. Take it away. Build the wall of books about 10 centimetres in front of the speaker, 30 centimetres tall and wide enough to hide it. Read twice. Take it away. Then stand the thick blanket upright, close to the speaker, held by a chair. Read twice. Write all the numbers.
flow.say: Same sound, same place. Only the thing in the way changes. Which one will you trust to protect a baby's sleep?
flow.kid: Put a paper, then a wall of books, then a blanket in the way. Read each twice.

ask.q: Which barrier cut the sound most, and which cut it least?
good: The answer from the table, such as the books or the blanket the most and the paper the least.
An answer that links a thicker, heavier or softer barrier with a bigger drop.

flow.parent: These are estimates, not measured results. Expect a drop of about 0 to 2 decibels for the paper, and perhaps 3 to 10 for books or a blanket. Sound also bends over the top and round the sides of a barrier, so make it taller than the speaker and wide enough. If all readings stay within 2 decibels of the start, check that the barrier is close to the speaker and has no gaps.

flow.do: Work out the drop for each change: the starting middle reading minus the new middle reading. Put the five changes in order from the biggest drop to the smallest, and draw a bar for each. Then ask: which one could you use at a loud function? Which could you use for a street?
flow.say: Which lever cut the most? Is it the one you guessed?
flow.kid: Work out each drop. Draw a bar for each. Which is biggest?

ask.q: The test is for a speaker in a room. What might be different for a bus horn on a road?
good: A horn is much louder and comes from far away, and the sound bends round barriers.
A road is open, so there is little bounce from walls, and a barrier has to be tall and solid.

flow.parent: This test cannot show how a barrier works for low or sudden sounds, or outdoors. Engineers still test those in the field. If a result surprised you, tell your child that surprises are the point.
flow.think: Which lever would you pull first to protect your own ears at a loud function, and which could you not pull at all?

activities.title: Wanted or not: sort the sounds of your day
activities.context: In this activity you sort the sounds around you by whether you want them. The same sound can be wanted by one person and unwanted by another. It shows that noise is a judgement, not a measurement.

materials.item: paper cut into 12 small slips
a pencil
a sheet of paper folded into four boxes

schedule.what: Listen for 2 minutes, write the sounds, sort them into four boxes, then find sounds that people sort differently.

activities.record: Keep the folded sheet with the sounds in their four boxes. Star the sounds where two people disagreed.

setup.art: A child sitting by a window with eyes closed and a pencil and paper slips on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still for 2 minutes with your eyes closed and listen.

setup.art: A sheet folded into four boxes labelled wanted and loud, wanted and quiet, unwanted and loud, unwanted and quiet, with slips in them.
setup.caption: 2. Write one sound on each slip. Sort the slips into the four boxes.

setup.art: A parent and a child each holding a slip with a different box in mind, pointing at different boxes.
setup.caption: 3. Swap boxes with a grown-up and find the sounds you placed differently.

flow.do: Sit still in a room with a window for two minutes. Close your eyes and count every different sound you hear on your fingers. Open your eyes and write each sound on its own slip, up to twelve.
flow.say: Close your eyes. How many different sounds can you find? Count them on your fingers.
flow.kid: Sit still for 2 minutes. Count the sounds. Write each on a slip.
flow.parent: If the room is too quiet to find 6 sounds, include the ones inside you, such as breathing, and the ones far away. Younger children can draw the sound instead of writing.

flow.do: Fold a sheet of paper into four boxes. Label them: wanted and loud, wanted and quiet, not wanted and loud, not wanted and quiet. Sort each slip into one box.
flow.say: Which sounds did you want to hear, and which would you switch off if you could? Put each in a box.
flow.kid: Sort the slips into the four boxes.

ask.q: Which box has the most slips, and which has the fewest?
good: Any honest count, with a thought about why.
An answer that notices that loud and unwanted sounds are not the only kind that bother people.

flow.do: Show your boxes to a parent, or a friend or older relative if you have one. Ask them to sort the same slips in their own four boxes without looking at yours. Compare. Put a star on every sound that was put into different boxes by the two of you.
flow.say: Where did we put the same sound in different boxes? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Sort the same slips again with another person. Star the sounds you placed differently.

ask.q: Why did the same sound go in different boxes?
good: Because people want different things at different times, such as a mixer-grinder at 7 in the morning.
Because who is listening, when and why matters as much as how strong the sound is.

flow.parent: Common differences: a child's own music, a baby's crying, a neighbour's festival song, a crow, a vendor's call. Do not argue about who is right. The point is that both are.

flow.do: Choose one starred sound. Write down two people who might sort it differently and what each would say. Then, together, think of one thing that could make it wanted for both.
flow.say: Think of two people who would sort that sound differently. What could make it better for both?
flow.kid: Write two people who would disagree about a starred sound. Think of one fix.
flow.think: A meter gives one number for a sound. What would you need to ask to find out whether it is noise?

activities.title: Feel the beat: sound through the hands, the table and the floor
activities.context: In this activity you feel the shaking of sound with your hands, your throat and the floor. You find out how a person who cannot hear can still take in a drum. It shows that sound is vibration, which is felt as well as heard.

materials.item: a phone or small speaker that can play a steady drum beat or a bass tune
2 balloons, blown up
a wooden or steel table

activities.safety: Keep the volume at the level of ordinary talk. Do not press a speaker against your ear or place a balloon between a speaker and an ear.

schedule.what: Feel the hum in your throat, the table and a balloon while a steady beat plays, and compare.

activities.record: Draw three hands on a page, one for the throat, one for the table and one for the balloon. Write beside each what the shaking felt like.

setup.art: A child with two fingers resting lightly on her own throat while humming.
setup.caption: 1. Hum and feel your throat shake.

setup.art: A child's flat palms resting on a wooden table with a small speaker beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Rest your palms on the table while a steady beat plays.

setup.art: A child holding a blown-up balloon lightly in both hands near a speaker with soft sound lines.
setup.caption: 3. Hold a balloon near the speaker and feel the beat in it.

flow.do: Rest two fingers lightly on your throat and hum a low note, then a high note. Next, hum with your hand on top of your head.
flow.say: Can you feel the shaking? Is it the same for a low hum and a high hum?
flow.kid: Hum with your fingers on your throat. Try a high note and a low note.

ask.q: Where did you feel the shaking, and was it different for low and high?
good: In the throat, and sometimes the chest or head. The low note shakes more.
Any honest description of where they felt it.

flow.do: Put a small speaker or phone on a wooden table. Play a steady drum beat at the volume of ordinary talk. Rest both flat palms on the table. Then rest your bare feet on the floor. Close your eyes and try to feel the beat.
flow.say: Is the table shaking? Can you tell where the beat is without hearing it?
flow.kid: Put both palms flat on the table while the beat plays. Feel the shaking.
flow.parent: Use a steady beat from a drum or a bass tune. A tune with deep notes is felt best. If the speaker is on a hard surface, the whole table shakes, which is why a drummer feels a drum in the floor.

flow.do: Blow up a balloon and hold it lightly with both hands, close to the speaker but not touching it. Feel the beat in the balloon. Try the same with the balloon against your chest.
flow.say: The balloon is full of air, and the air is being shaken. Can you feel each beat?
flow.kid: Hold a balloon near the speaker. Feel the beat in it.

ask.q: What did the beat feel like in your hands?
good: A small pulse or throb with each beat.
A tickle, a buzz or a shake.

flow.do: Talk about this: A girl who has been deaf since she was born stands barefoot beside a drum. What might she feel, and what might she hear? Share it with a parent, then write one sentence.
flow.say: Evelyn Glennie is a Scottish percussionist who has been deaf since she was a child. She plays barefoot so that she can feel the music through the floor. What do you think she feels?
flow.kid: Write one sentence about what a deaf person can feel in a drum.
flow.think: Is feeling the drum with your hands a kind of hearing, or a different thing?
flow.parent: Scientists still discuss whether feeling a drum is a kind of hearing. Many Deaf people would say they feel music fully.

activities.title: Two ears, one bell: can you point to where a sound is?
activities.context: In this activity a helper makes a soft sound from different places around you and you point to it with your eyes closed. It shows how two ears let us find where a sound comes from, which is what a good warning depends on.

materials.item: a steel spoon and a steel tumbler, or a small bell
a helper
a scarf to cover the eyes, or just closed eyes

activities.safety: Make only soft sounds, never near an ear.

schedule.what: Point to a soft sound from 8 places with two ears, then with one ear gently covered, and compare.

activities.record: Make a table with two columns: both ears and one ear covered. Put a tick each time you pointed correctly. Write the two totals.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair with eyes shut and a helper standing behind her tapping a tumbler with a spoon.
setup.caption: 1. Sit with your eyes closed. A helper taps softly from different places.

setup.art: A top-down drawing of eight places around a chair, numbered, with an arrow pointing to the helper's position.
setup.caption: 2. Point to each tap. The helper notes if you were right.

setup.art: The same child with one palm resting gently over one ear while pointing.
setup.caption: 3. Cover one ear with a palm and try again.

flow.do: Sit your child on a chair with eyes closed. Stand 2 big steps away. Tap the tumbler softly with the spoon, at the volume of a quiet knock. Ask your child to point. Practise twice.
flow.say: Close your eyes. I will tap somewhere. Point to where you think it is.
flow.kid: Sit with your eyes closed. Point to each soft tap.
flow.parent: The tap should be soft. A table-top knock is about right. Do not tap close to the ear.

flow.do: Tap from 8 places in turn: front, back, left, right, above, below, and two in between. Mix the order. After each tap, write a tick if your child pointed within a hand's width of the right place. Write a cross if not.
flow.say: Where is this one? Point first, and open your eyes at the end to check.
flow.kid: Point to each tap with your eyes closed.

ask.q: Which places were hardest to point to?
good: Straight ahead, straight behind or above, where the sound reaches both ears at the same time.
Any honest answer. Sounds on the side are usually easier.

flow.do: Now ask your child to rest one palm gently over one ear. Do the same eight taps, in a different order. Count the ticks again.
flow.say: Now one ear is covered. Is it as easy? Which places are hardest now?
flow.kid: Cover one ear with a palm. Point to each tap again.

ask.q: Why is it harder to find a sound with one ear covered?
good: A sound reaches one ear a tiny bit sooner and louder than the other. The brain uses that to tell where it is.
With one ear, the brain has no difference to compare.

flow.parent: A sound from far to one side reaches the nearer ear up to about half a thousandth of a second before the other. The brain compares the two. A siren that sweeps up and down gives more to compare than one steady note.

flow.do: Swap places so that your child taps and you point. Then talk about it: why do a train's horn, an ambulance siren and a smoke alarm all sound so different from a steady hum?
flow.say: A good warning has to be heard and also found. What kind of sound is easy to find?
flow.kid: Swap with your helper and tap for them. Talk about warnings.
flow.think: Why might a siren sweep up and down rather than stay on one note?

activities.title: Warning duel: which sound do you notice and find first?
activities.context: In this activity you make four warning sounds from things at home. You test which one stands out over a background sound, which one can be found and which one has a meaning. It shows what makes a warning work.

materials.item: a radio or a phone playing quiet talking at the volume of a conversation
a steel spoon and tumbler
a rubber band stretched over a bowl
a whistle or a small bell
a helper in the next room
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Use the sounds softly and keep them away from the ears.

schedule.what: Play four warnings over a background and score each for standing out, being found and having a meaning.

activities.record: Fill a table with four rows, one for each sound, and three columns: noticed, found, meaning. Give each a score from 1 to 3.

setup.art: A radio on a shelf playing quiet talking, with four sound-makers laid on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Play a quiet background. Choose four ways to make a warning sound.

setup.art: A child in one room and a helper in the next room with a doorway between them, the helper sounding a bell.
setup.caption: 2. Sound each from the next room. The listener says when they notice it.

setup.art: A table with four rows and three columns, with scores written in.
setup.caption: 3. Score each for being noticed, being found and having a meaning.

flow.do: Put a radio or phone playing quiet talk in one room at the volume of a conversation. Lay out four sound-makers. Use the spoon on the tumbler, the plucked rubber band, the whistle or bell, and one of your own such as clapping. Agree on a meaning for each, such as 'come to dinner' or 'fire'.
flow.say: These four things will be our warnings. What do you think each one means? Which will be noticed first?
flow.kid: Choose four warning sounds. Give each a meaning. Guess which is noticed first.
flow.parent: Do not use a real alarm, a loud whistle or anything that could frighten a baby or a pet.

flow.do: Ask your child to listen in the room with the radio, doing a puzzle. Sound the warnings from the next room, one at a time, with a gap of about 30 seconds. Your child says 'now' when they notice each one. Write which was noticed and how quickly.
flow.say: Do your puzzle. Say 'now' as soon as you notice something new.
flow.kid: Do a puzzle. Say 'now' when you notice a new sound.

ask.q: Which sound did you notice first, and what was special about it?
good: The one that was sharp, high or sudden and different from the talking.
An answer that notices the warning was different from the background.

flow.do: Sound each warning again from a different place in the room. Ask your child to point to it with eyes closed. Write a tick for each one found.
flow.say: Can you tell where each one is? Which one is easiest?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Point to each warning.

ask.q: Which warning was easiest to find, and why do you think so?
good: The one with the sharper sound, which reached one ear before the other.
The one that kept changing pitch or repeating.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what each sound means without being told. Then score each warning from 1 to 3 for standing out, being found and having a meaning. Talk about why a smoke alarm is shrill on purpose and why the pressure cooker's whistle works.
flow.say: A warning with no meaning warns nobody. Which of ours had a meaning the others could learn?
flow.kid: Say what each sound means. Score all four.
flow.think: If a warning sounds all day long, what happens to it?

activities.title: Silence hunt: find the quietest place and listen to what is left
activities.context: In this activity you look for the quietest place in your home, measure it, and listen for what is still there. It shows that a living listener never meets complete silence.

materials.item: a phone with a sound-meter app, or just your ears
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Visit three places, listen for 2 minutes in each, measure each and list every sound left.

activities.record: List the three places, the reading for each (if you have a meter) and every sound you heard in each. Mark any sounds from inside your own body.

setup.art: A child sitting in a built-in cupboard with the door open, holding a phone and a paper list.
setup.caption: 1. Choose three quiet places in your home.

setup.art: A child listening with closed eyes, with a timer showing 2 minutes.
setup.caption: 2. Listen in each for 2 minutes and list every sound.

setup.art: A page with three places listed and a sound list under each, with a few in a circle for body sounds.
setup.caption: 3. Circle the sounds that were from inside you.

flow.do: Choose three quiet places in your home, such as a room with the door shut, a cupboard or a bathroom. Predict which will be the quietest.
flow.say: Which place do you think will be the quietest? What would you hear there?
flow.kid: Pick three quiet places. Guess which is the quietest.
flow.parent: Stay in rooms. Do not shut a child in a cupboard. A built-in cupboard with the door open is enough.

flow.do: Sit in each place for 2 minutes with your eyes closed, and write every sound you can find. If you have a sound meter, take the 30-second average reading as well. Include faint sounds like a fridge, a far-off horn, your own breath or a ringing in your ears.
flow.say: Listen for 2 minutes. Is there ever a moment with no sound at all?
flow.kid: Sit in each place for 2 minutes. Write all the sounds.

ask.q: Did you find a place with no sound at all?
good: No. There was always something, even if faint.
Any honest answer, with the faint sounds named.

flow.do: Circle every sound on your list that came from inside your body, such as breathing, a heartbeat or a thin ringing. Press your palms gently over your ears in the quietest place and listen to the low rumble inside.
flow.say: Which sounds were not from outside? Whose sounds are they?
flow.kid: Circle the sounds that came from your own body.
flow.parent: The low rumble heard with palms over the ears is partly made by the tiny shaking of muscles in the hands, arms and head. John Cage heard two sounds in a silent room at Harvard in 1951.

flow.do: Compare your quietest place with the limit of 40 decibels at night in a silence zone, if you measured. Then ask: was the quietest place really silent?
flow.say: Is there a place on Earth with no sound at all?
flow.kid: Write one sentence about whether you found silence.
flow.think: If a very quiet room still has your breath and your blood in it, is silence a place or a feeling?

projects.title: My week of listening: how many hours, how loud?
projects.context: In this project you log a week of your own listening, through earphones and speakers. You work out whether it fits the World Health Organization's weekly allowance for a child. It shows that the dose for the ear depends on both how loud it is and for how long.

materials.item: a sheet of squared paper for a weekly chart
a pencil
a phone or earphones, if you use them
a clock or the phone's own screen-time or listening record

schedule.what: Draw the weekly chart and write a guess for the week's total.
Log yesterday's listening hours and the volume check.
Log the listening hours and the volume check.
Log the listening hours and the volume check.
Log the listening hours and the volume check.
Log the listening hours and the volume check.
Add up, compare with the allowance and make a family plan.

projects.record: Keep a chart with a column for each day. For each day write the hours of listening through earphones and the hours through a speaker. Add a tick if you could hear someone speaking to you at arm's length. At the end, write the weekly total and one change you will make.

setup.art: A weekly chart with seven columns, one for each day, and rows for earphone hours, speaker hours and an arm's-length check.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the chart and guess the week's total.

setup.art: A child wearing earphones with a parent speaking to her at arm's length, the child looking puzzled.
setup.caption: 2. Do the arm's-length check: can you hear someone speaking to you?

setup.art: A bar chart of the days with a line across it marked 40 hours.
setup.caption: 3. Add up the week and compare with the allowance.

flow.do: Draw a chart with seven columns for the week. Make one row for the hours of listening with earphones. Make a second row for hours with a speaker or television. Make a third row for the arm's-length check. Write your guess for the total for the week.
flow.say: How many hours do you think you listen through earphones in a week? Write a guess and do not change it.
flow.kid: Draw the weekly chart. Write a guess for the week's total.
flow.parent: Younger children can use coloured blocks for each half hour. If the child does not use earphones, count the hours of television, music or class sound instead, and note that this is the one to compare.

flow.do: On each of days 2 to 6, spend 5 minutes in the evening. Fill in the hours of the day before from memory or from the phone's own record. Do the arm's-length check: wear the earphones at the usual volume and ask someone to speak to you from an arm's length away. Tick if you can hear them clearly. If you cannot, turn the volume down until you can.
flow.say: When did you wear earphones yesterday? For how long? At the usual volume, could you hear me at arm's length?
flow.kid: Each evening, fill in your listening hours. Do the arm's-length check.

ask.q: Could you hear someone speaking at arm's length, and if not, what does that tell you?
good: The sound was louder than the voice, so the earphones were too loud.
Any honest answer, with the turning down noted.

flow.wait: Do this each evening for five days
flow.parent: Many phones show listening levels in their health or settings pages. Look at them together if they are available. Phone volume is not a true decibel number, so the arm's-length check is a practical test, not a measurement.

flow.do: On the last day, add up the week's hours. Compare with the allowance. For a child it is up to 40 hours a week at 75 decibels. Every 3 decibels louder halves the safe time. Work out, if your earphones were at 81 decibels, how many hours would be safe (40 halved twice is 10). Write a plan for your family with one thing you will keep and one you will change. If your family goes to loud functions, add foam earplugs to the plan.
flow.say: The World Health Organization says 75 decibels for up to 40 hours is the weekly allowance for a child. If the sound is 3 decibels louder, what happens to the hours?
flow.kid: Add up the week. Work out the safe hours at 81 decibels. Write one change.

ask.q: What is the safe time at 81 decibels, and how did you work it out?
good: 10 hours. 81 is 6 decibels more than 75, which is two steps of 3, so 40 halved twice is 10.
Any answer that halves the time for each 3 decibels.

flow.think: Which is easier to change for your ears, the volume or the hours?
flow.parent: The weekly allowance is a guide for safe listening. Because the real decibel level depends on the earphones, treat the hours as a rough guide and the arm's-length check as the daily rule.

projects.safety: Never turn the volume up for the arm's-length check. If someone at arm's length cannot be heard clearly, turn the volume down, and take the earphones out if the sound is ever painful.

projects.title: A street noise report: measure it, ask the neighbours, suggest a fix
projects.context: In this project you study one noise on your own street. You measure it by day and by night, ask three neighbours how it affects them, and suggest fixes. It shows that noise is both a measurement and a matter of people with different needs.

materials.item: a phone with a sound-meter app
paper, a pencil and a clipboard or hard book
a grown-up to go with you

projects.safety: Stay on the pavement or at your gate and go with a grown-up. Do not go near traffic.

schedule.what: Choose the noise and write what you expect.
Measure by day, at two times.
A grown-up measures it at night.
Ask three neighbours, including one who sees it differently.
Write the report and three fixes.

projects.record: Make a one-page report. Put in the noise's name, the readings by day and by night, and what three neighbours said. Then give three fixes, one for the source, one for the path or distance and one for the time.

setup.art: A child on a pavement with a grown-up, holding a phone towards a street scene with a loudspeaker on a pole.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one noise on your street and measure it.

setup.art: A child talking to a woman at a doorway with a notebook in her hands.
setup.caption: 2. Ask three neighbours what they think of it.

setup.art: A single page headed Street noise report with a table of readings and three fixes listed.
setup.caption: 3. Write the report and the three fixes.

flow.do: Choose one noise on your street that bothers people, such as horns at a junction, a loudspeaker, a generator or building work. Write what you expect to find: how loud it is by day and by night, and who minds it most.
flow.say: Which noise on our street do people talk about? Who do you think minds it most, and who minds it least?
flow.kid: Choose one noise. Write what you expect.
flow.parent: Pick a noise that is regular so it can be measured again. Avoid choosing a single neighbour's private matter, which could cause a quarrel. A road, a junction, a generator or a building site is better.

flow.do: Stand at the same place on the pavement or at your gate, with a grown-up, at two times in the day. Take the 30-second average twice at each time. Write the numbers and what you could hear.
flow.say: Is it louder at one time of the day? What makes the number go up?
flow.kid: Measure twice at two times of day. Write the numbers.

flow.do: A grown-up measures the same noise from the same place after 10 at night, if it is there then. Write the numbers. If the noise is not there at night, write that and the quiet reading.
flow.say: At night, the limit for homes is lower. How does your number compare?
flow.kid: A grown-up measures at night. Write the number.
flow.parent: Compare with 55 by day and 45 at night for residential areas, or 50 and 40 within 100 metres of a school, hospital or court. Remember the phone's reading is a guide, not proof.

flow.do: With a grown-up, ask three neighbours: how does this noise affect you, when is it worst, and what would help? Include at least one person with a different view. This could be a night-shift worker, a street vendor, a shopkeeper or a person who runs the noise. Write the answers in their own words.
flow.say: Listen first. You are not trying to win an argument. What does each person say they need?
flow.kid: Ask three neighbours the same three questions. Write what they say.

ask.q: Did all three give the same answer? Why or why not?
good: No. Different people need different things at different times.
An answer that notices a sleeping baby and a shop owner may want opposite things.

flow.do: Write the report on one page. Include the noise, the numbers and what the neighbours said. Then add three fixes, one for each lever. Make it quieter at the source, put distance or a barrier in its path, and change the time. Check that each fix would work for the people you asked.
flow.say: A good fix helps the person who is hurt and does not unfairly hurt the person who makes the sound. Can yours do both?
flow.kid: Write the page. Add three fixes, one for each lever.
flow.think: Whose job is it to fix a noise that belongs to everybody?
flow.parent: If the child would like, help them to share the report with the building's residents' association or the local ward office. Only share names with permission.

challenges.title: A quiet classroom beside a busy road
challenges.context: This is a design problem. You build a shoebox classroom and play traffic sound outside it. You design ways to lower the sound inside by at least 6 decibels while letting in light and air. It shows how engineers quieten a place with a barrier, a soft lining and a gap that sound cannot pass.
challenges.problem: A school stands beside a busy road. The windows must stay open for air and light on hot days. Find a way to lower the traffic sound reaching the children inside by at least 6 decibels. Or lower it to a level where talk is easy to hear. Do not close the windows completely. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use only things you can find at home. A phone with a meter app is allowed.
The classroom must still let in light, shown by a window you can see through. It must also let in air, shown by a gap at least as big as your thumb.
The traffic sound must stay at the volume of ordinary talk, never louder.
Test each design at least twice and write the readings down, and say how much each lowered the level.
materials: a shoebox or a small cardboard box with a window cut in one side
a phone playing a steady traffic or fan sound, placed 30 centimetres outside the window
a phone with a sound-meter app placed inside the box
scraps of cloth, cotton wool, paper, egg cartons, a strip of card and tape
scissors, used by a grown-up, and tape

setup.art: A shoebox with a window cut in one side, a phone playing traffic outside it and a phone measuring inside.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a window in a shoebox. Put one phone outside to play traffic and one phone inside to measure.

setup.art: A shoebox with a strip of cardboard standing a little way outside the window as a barrier.
setup.caption: 2. Try the usual fixes first: a barrier outside and a soft lining inside.

setup.art: A card tube bent into a zigzag with a gap at each bend, fitted over the window.
setup.caption: 3. Try a surprising fix: a zigzag air channel that lets air through but bends sound round corners.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts a window about 8 centimetres square in one side of the box. Put the measuring phone inside, and the playing phone about 30 centimetres outside the window. Read the 30-second average twice with nothing else. This is the starting level.
flow.say: Is the traffic loud inside the box? What would you try first?
flow.kid: Cut a window in the box. Play traffic outside. Read the level inside.
flow.parent: Cutting is for a grown-up. Keep the volume low, at the level of talk, so that nothing is harmful. Take a fresh reading if the number jumps.

flow.do: Try the usual fixes. Stand a strip of card or a hardback book as a barrier between the playing phone and the window. Line the inside with cloth or egg cartons. Close the window partly. Read twice for each fix and write the numbers.
flow.say: Which fix lowered the sound most? Did any of them stop light or air?
flow.kid: Try a barrier, a soft lining and a half-closed window. Read each twice.

ask.q: Which fix gave the biggest drop, and what did it cost in light or air?
good: The answer from the numbers, with a note about light or air.
An answer that notices a closed window blocks air as well as sound.

flow.do: Try a surprising fix. Roll thin card into a tube about the width of a thumb and bend it into a zigzag. Fit it so that air must pass through the bends to reach the window. Line the inside of the tube with cloth. Read twice. Then try your own idea, for example a barrier that is tall and a lining that is thick.
flow.say: A silencer for air lets air through but makes sound bounce around until it fades. Can you make one?
flow.kid: Make a zigzag air channel with a soft lining. Try it. Read twice.

ask.q: Did the zigzag let air through, and how much did it cut the sound?
good: Yes, if the channel stayed open. It cut the sound by a few decibels or more.
Any honest answer with the numbers.

flow.parent: Real buildings use this idea, called a silencer or baffle, in air vents. It lets air pass and makes sound bounce around until it fades.

flow.do: Compare all your designs. For each, write the drop in decibels and whether it kept light and air. Choose the best compromise and say why. Note that no model shows what happens outdoors or for sudden bangs.
flow.say: Which would you choose for a real school? What would you give up?
flow.kid: Write each drop. Choose the best design. Say what it gave up.
flow.think: Is the best way to quieten a school to build it better, or to make the road quieter?

general: Put a solid barrier between the road and the windows, as tall as the windows.
Line the room's walls and ceiling with soft material so that sound that gets in does not bounce about.
Plant a thick belt of trees and bushes, which also hides the road from view, and move noisy rooms away from the road side.
Fit double windows with a gap between them, and close the ones that face the road on the worst days.
creative: Build a zigzag air channel with a soft lining, so that air can pass and sound is bent round corners until it fades.
Move the quiet rooms to the far side of the building. Use the road side for stores and corridors.
Slow the drivers down in front of the school with a speed bump and a painted 'No Horn' board. That cuts the source, not the path.
challenges.your_turn: Build your own design and test it. How many decibels did it take off? Which idea of yours would you want to try in a real classroom?

challenges.title: A warning for a person who cannot hear it
challenges.context: This is a design problem. Many people cannot hear a smoke alarm or a doorbell, so you design a warning that works through light or touch. It shows what a warning needs to do, and that sound is only one way of carrying it.
challenges.problem: A Deaf neighbour, asleep in bed, needs to be woken by a smoke alarm in the next room. Design a warning that reaches her without sound and that will wake a sleeping person. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Never connect anything to the mains electricity or a socket. Use a phone, a torch or a battery toy.
Nothing must touch a flame or anything hot.
The warning must work in the dark and not depend on the person looking in one direction.
Test it with a grown-up who is sitting with eyes closed, not asleep, and write whether they noticed it.
materials: a phone with a stopwatch or a vibrate setting
a torch or a small lamp that runs on batteries
a long string or cord, a steel tumbler, a spoon
a toy that vibrates, or a phone on vibrate

setup.art: A grown-up sitting with eyes closed on a bed, a child at the door pressing a phone that makes a torch flash.
setup.caption: 1. Test what a person with eyes closed notices: a flashing torch.

setup.art: A phone on vibrate placed under a pillow, with a pad of folded towel around it.
setup.caption: 2. Test a vibrating phone under a pillow.

setup.art: A string running from the child at the door to a tumbler and spoon tied by the bedpost.
setup.caption: 3. Test your own invention.

flow.do: Write down three things a sleeping person's body can sense besides sound: light on closed eyelids, touch, and shaking. Choose one way to carry the warning. Say how it must start at the same moment as a smoke alarm.
flow.say: What are all the ways you could wake someone without a sound? Which would you choose?
flow.kid: Write three ways to wake someone with no sound.

ask.q: Which senses besides hearing can wake a sleeping person?
good: Touch, shaking and bright light on the eyelids.
Any honest answer with a reason.

flow.do: Try the usual fixes. Ask a grown-up to sit on a bed with eyes closed, or a child to sit with eyes closed on a chair. Flash a torch on the closed eyes from the door. Put a phone on vibrate under a pillow and call it. Write whether the person noticed it, and how fast.
flow.say: Did the flashing light get noticed? Did the shaking? Which was faster?
flow.kid: Test a flashing torch and a vibrating phone. Write what was noticed.
flow.parent: Never wake a real sleeping person for this test, and never test it on a baby. Use a grown-up with eyes closed. Do not use a very bright torch at the eyes. Use a soft light, and flash it slowly, no more than about twice a second. Do not use a flashing light on anyone who has epilepsy or gets seizures from lights.

flow.do: Try a surprising fix. Tie a long string to a steel tumbler or a toy on the bedpost. A gentle pull from the door should make it shake or rattle the bed. Or put the vibrating phone in a small bag tied to the pillow. Test and write what was noticed.
flow.say: A string can carry a shake across the room. Can you use it?
flow.kid: Build a string that shakes the bed. Test it.

ask.q: Did your invention work, and what would make it better?
good: Yes or no, with a reason, and an idea to make it better.
Any honest answer that looks for a fix.

flow.do: Compare the ways. For each, write whether it works in the dark and whether it works if the person turns over. Also write whether the alarm can set it off. Choose the best and say why.
flow.say: Which one would you trust to wake your own family?
flow.kid: Compare your ways. Choose the best.
flow.think: A warning must reach the person. Does it have to be a sound?

general: A bright flashing light that starts when the alarm sounds, placed where the person sleeps.
A small vibrating pad under the pillow or the mattress that shakes when the alarm sounds.
A neighbour or a relative who calls and checks, as part of a plan.
creative: A string from the doorway to a bell or a tumbler tied to the bed.
A phone set to vibrate on a wooden bedstead, which carries the shaking along the frame.
A warning that does several things together, such as lights, shaking and a fan of air on the face.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own warning for a person who cannot hear it. Which sense does it use? What would make you trust it to work every time?

games.title: Quiet Street: a team card game about bringing a street's sound down
games.context: In this team card game, sounds arrive on a street one by one. The players use fix cards to bring the street's total level under a limit. It shows how decibels combine, and why a quieter source, more distance or a barrier each help.

setup.caption: 1. Draw the street with 5 boxes. Choose a zone card and put it above the street.

setup.art: Two piles of cards, sounds and fixes, with a hand of four fix cards held by each player.
setup.caption: 2. Shuffle the sound cards and the fix cards into two piles. Deal four fix cards to each player.

setup.art: A street with three sound cards laid out and a fix card placed under one of them.
setup.caption: 3. Each round, a sound card joins the street. Players then play fix cards on the sounds.
