printables.title: 4 zone cards
items: Silence zone. The street may be no louder than 50 decibels. Very hard.
Residential area. The street may be no louder than 55 decibels. Hard.
Commercial area. The street may be no louder than 65 decibels. Medium.
Industrial area. The street may be no louder than 75 decibels. Easy.

printables.title: 1 adding table card
items: Adding two sounds. Take the louder level and add this much. If the two levels are the same, add 3. If they differ by 1, 2 or 3, add 2. If they differ by 4 to 9, add 1. If they differ by 10 or more, add 0. Start with the loudest sound and add the others one at a time, from the next loudest to the quietest. These are rounded, so the answers are close and not exact.

rules: This is a team game. All the players win together or lose together. You can play alone, with a parent or with friends.

Choose a zone card and put it above the street. For one or two players, choose Commercial. For three or four, choose Residential. Use an easier zone if the street keeps winning against you and a harder one if you win every time.
Shuffle the 12 sound cards and put them in a pile. Shuffle the 20 fix cards and deal four to each player. Put the rest in a pile for drawing.

Each round has two steps. First, turn the top sound card over and put it in the next empty box on the street. Second, the players take turns. Each plays one fix card from their hand on any sound in the street and puts it under that card. Then each draws a new card to bring their hand back to four. A player playing alone may play two fix cards on their turn. Then the next round starts.

A fix card changes the level of the sound it is placed under: take that many decibels off. A 'Stop it for now' card takes the sound out of the street altogether. Several fix cards can go on one sound. You can also choose not to play a card.

After the fifth sound has joined the street and the players have played their cards for that round, the game ends. Work out the street's level with the adding table card. Start with the loudest sound after its fixes and add each next one, loudest to quietest.
If the street's level is the same as or lower than the zone card's number, the team wins. If not, the street is too loud and the team loses. Talk about which fix cards would have helped.
If the fix pile runs out, nobody draws any more, and the players use the cards in their hands.
Say aloud after the game: which fix did we use most, and which could a real street use?

flow.do: Cut out the cards or write each on a slip of paper. Draw a long street on a big sheet of paper with 5 boxes along it for the sounds. Shuffle the sound cards and the fix cards separately.
flow.say: This is a street with a limit. Sounds will come, and we will fix them together.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Draw the street with 5 boxes. Shuffle.
flow.parent: Print the cards from this lesson. Cutting is for a grown-up if the child is under 8. Keep the cards in an envelope. The decibel numbers are made up, but realistic.

flow.do: Choose a zone card and put it over the street. Deal four fix cards to each player. Read the adding table card together and try one sum: one sound of 80 and one of 80 make 83. One of 80 and one of 75 make 81.
flow.say: Two horns together are not double. Let us try adding 80 and 80. What do you think the answer is?
flow.kid: Read the adding table. Try 80 and 80.

ask.q: Two sounds of 80 decibels together make how many decibels?
good: 83. Twice the energy is 3 decibels more, and does not double the number.
About 83, not 160.

flow.do: Play five rounds. Each round, turn over a sound card and put it in the next box. Then each player plays one fix card under a sound and draws a card. Talk with your team about which sounds to fix first and why.
flow.say: Which sound should we fix first? Why is the loudest one the one that matters most?
flow.kid: Play the rounds. Talk about which sound to fix.

ask.q: Why is it better to fix the loudest sound than the quietest one?
good: Because the loudest sound sets the street's level, and a quiet one adds almost nothing to it.
Because adding a 60 to a 90 changes almost nothing.

flow.do: After the fifth round, work out the street's level with the adding table. Check it against the zone card. Talk about the result.
flow.say: Is the street under the limit? What did the team do that worked best?
flow.kid: Work out the street's level. Check it against the zone.
flow.think: Which fix would be easy for a real street, and which would be hard?

games.title: Higher or lower: the decibel ladder
games.context: In this card game you guess whether the next sound is louder or quieter than the one before. You learn where everyday sounds sit on the decibel ladder. It shows the real sizes of sounds, from rustling leaves to a cracker.

setup.art: A deck of 14 cards face down, with one card turned up showing a sound name, and a player pointing.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the 14 cards and put them face down in a pile. Turn the top card face up.

setup.art: A hand turning a card over to reveal 'About 60 decibels' on the back.
setup.caption: 2. Say 'higher' or 'lower'. Turn the new card over to check.

printables.title: 14 sound cards, with the decibel number on the back

items.f: A busy road, seen from the pavement
An auto horn from 2 metres away
A road drill from 2 metres away
A cracker at the legal limit, 4 metres away

printables.title: Score sheet, to copy by hand
items: One row for each player. In each row, put a mark for every right guess.

rules: Shuffle the 14 cards and put them face down. Turn the top card over, face up, and read its name. Do not read the back yet.
The first player says whether the next card's sound is louder or quieter than the one showing, 'higher' or 'lower'. Then the card is turned over and the back is read out.
If the guess is right, the player earns one mark. If the two cards show the same number, any guess is right.

A player may also earn a bonus mark when the two cards are 10 or 20 decibels apart. The player says how many times more sound energy the louder card carries. For 10 decibels it is 10 times, and for 20 decibels it is 100 times.
The new card is now the one showing. Pass the turn to the next player.
When the pile is finished, count the marks. The player with the most marks wins. Players alone try to beat their last score.
Shuffle the cards and play again. A second time, try to remember where each sound goes on the ladder.

flow.do: Cut out the 14 cards and write each sound on the front and its number on the back. Shuffle and put them face down in a pile. Turn the top card up.
flow.say: Where would a whisper go on a ladder of sounds? Which of these do you think is the loudest?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle. Turn one up.
flow.parent: The numbers are rounded and different meters show different readings. The cracker at 1 metre is worked out from the legal limit of 125 decibels at 4 metres. Every halving of distance adds about 6 decibels, so two halvings make about 12 more, or 137.

flow.do: Play the pile through. Each player says 'higher' or 'lower', the next card is turned over, and the back is read out. Give a bonus mark for saying how many times more sound energy the louder card has. This is for cards that are 10 or 20 decibels apart.
flow.say: Is the next sound louder or quieter? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Say higher or lower. Turn over the card.

ask.q: A card is 20 decibels louder than another. How many times more sound energy does it carry?
good: 100 times. Every 10 decibels is 10 times, and 20 is 10 times 10.
Roughly 100 times.

flow.do: Count the marks and talk about it. Which sounds surprised you? Where do the crackers sit compared with everyday sounds?
flow.say: Which sound was higher than you thought?
flow.kid: Count your marks. Which sound surprised you?
flow.think: The ladder goes from 20 to 137. Why can one number do the work of so many?

worksheets.title: Decibels, the ear and India's rules (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks that you can read decibel numbers, name the parts of the ear, and say what India's rules and the three levers do.

items.p: Which of these can a sound-level meter measure?
items.why: A meter measures strength in decibels. Whether a sound is noise is a judgement by the listener, so no meter can say it.

items.p: A whisper is about 30 decibels and ordinary talk about 60. Talk carries about ____ times the sound energy of a whisper.
items.why: The gap is 30 decibels. Every 10 decibels is 10 times the energy, so 30 decibels is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000.

items.p: Ten horns of 90 decibels each, sounding together, make roughly 100 decibels.
items.why: True. Ten times the energy adds 10 decibels. Doubling adds only about 3, so decibels do not add like ordinary numbers.

items.p: Match each part of the ear to what it does.
pairs: Holds the hair cells in liquid
Send a signal when their tufts bend
items.why: Sound is passed inwards from the eardrum, along the bones, into the liquid of the cochlea, and the hair cells turn the movement into signals.

items.p: Put the journey of a sound into the ear in order, first to last.
a: Three tiny bones pass the shaking on
The liquid in the cochlea moves
A nerve signal goes to the brain
items.why: Each step hands the shaking to the next, and the hair cells are the last place where shaking becomes a signal.

items.p: Sort each harm by where it happens.
items: a ringing heard after a loud wedding
Harm to the ear
a raised heartbeat while asleep as a lorry passes
Harm beyond the ear
losing high pitches around 4,000 hertz
Harm to the ear
falling behind in reading beside a noisy railway
Harm beyond the ear
higher stress chemicals in whales
Harm beyond the ear
items.why: Noise reaches the ear first, but it also raises the body's stress, breaks sleep and slows learning, and it affects other animals too.

items.p: Which kind of area has the lowest noise limits in India's rules?
items.why: A silence zone, the area within 100 metres of a hospital, school or court, has 50 decibels by day and 40 at night. Industrial areas are allowed the most.

items.p: A residential area's limit is 55 decibels by day and 45 at night. How many decibels lower is the night limit?
items.why: 55 − 45 = 10. Ten decibels means one tenth of the sound energy, so the night limit is much stricter than it looks.

items.p: A ball of cotton wool in the ear cuts sound as much as a well-fitted foam earplug.
items.why: False. Cotton wool cuts about 5 to 7 decibels. A well-fitted foam earplug cuts about 15 to 30.

items.p: Which of these protects the ear by changing the time?
opts: Leaving the function after an hour
items.why: Staying for less time lowers the dose. Walking away changes the path, and turning the volume down changes the source.

items.p: Your hearing feels normal the morning after a loud function. Does that prove no harm was done? Explain.
items.a: Not proven. In 2009, mice that passed hearing tests had lost up to half the links between hair cells and nerve. Whether this happens in people is still being debated, so a normal test does not prove there was no harm.
items.why: A strong answer says that a normal test and no harm are different things, and that scientists still argue about hidden hearing loss in people.

items.p: Why is a smoke alarm made shrill and unpleasant on purpose?
opts: So nobody can sleep through it
items.why: A warning has to be noticed over everything, even in sleep. A pleasant sound is easier to ignore.

items.p: Which is the odd one out and why? Broken sleep, raised blood pressure, tinnitus, stress chemicals in whales.
items.a: Tinnitus, because it is a harm to the ear. The other three are harms beyond the ear.
items.why: Noise acts on the whole body, and on other animals, as well as on the ear.

items.p: A friend reads 82 decibels on a phone and says, 'My neighbour is breaking the law.' What do you say?
items.a: Ask where and when it was measured, for how long, and which kind of area it is. Phone apps can be off by several decibels. The limits apply outside homes, and the zone and the time of day change the limit.
items.why: A good answer treats the number as a pointer, not proof, and asks about the place, the time and the kind of area.

items.p: A band with a loudspeaker marches past a hospital at noon.

views.who: A doctor at the hospital (an imagined view)
views.says: The area near a hospital is a silence zone for a reason. Sick people and new babies need quiet, and noise can harm them.

views.who: A member of the wedding procession (an imagined view)
views.says: A wedding comes once in a life. The band passes in a few minutes, and the road is public for everyone.

items.ask: What would you try before choosing a side?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer looks for a way that works for both, such as a different road, a quieter band near the hospital, or a shorter time.
items.why: Both views are real. The rules and the doctor protect people who cannot move away. The procession shows that a rule must also respect what people value.

items.p: Draw a hair cell before and after very loud sound. Show the tuft of hairs.
items.a: Two drawings of a cell with a tuft. The first has a neat, upright tuft. The second has a bent, flattened or broken tuft, or no cell at all.
items.why: Loud sound bends the tuft too far, and with enough sound the cell dies and is not replaced.

worksheets.title: Distance, dose and other animals (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to work out how sound changes with distance and time, and to think about animals and warnings.

items.p: A steady sound reads 96 decibels at 1 metre in the open. What does it read at 8 metres?
items.why: From 1 metre to 8 metres is three doublings (1, 2, 4, 8). Each doubling takes off about 6 decibels, so 96 − 18 = 78.

items.p: A child's safe listening is 40 hours a week at 75 decibels. At 81 decibels the safe time is ____ hours.
items.why: 81 is 6 decibels above 75, which is two steps of 3. Each step halves the time, so 40 → 20 → 10.

items.p: A hall of 40 children talking reads 80 decibels. What would 20 children talking the same way read?
items.why: Halving the number of equal sources takes off about 3 decibels, not half the number.

items.p: Noise-cancelling headphones work best on a sudden sharp horn.
items.why: False. They work best on steady, low sounds, such as an aeroplane's engine drone. A sudden or high sound changes too fast to cancel.

items.p: Match each living being to what scientists found.
pairs: Sings at a higher pitch in noisy cities
Had fewer stress chemicals when ship noise fell
Made more defence chemicals after chewing vibrations were played
Hides and shakes on cracker nights
items.why: Noise reaches many kinds of living beings, and each responds in a way that fits the body and the life.

items.p: Sort each way of protecting the ears by the lever it uses.
items: choosing a quieter mixer-grinder
The source
sitting at the back of the hall
The path
leaving after one hour
The time
shutting the window
The path
turning the volume down
The source
taking a quiet break after loud sound
The time
items.why: Source is where the sound is made, path is what lies between, and time is how long you stay. Each lowers the dose.

items.p: After a loud night you hear a faint ringing. What does this most likely show?
opts: The sound was more than the ear could take
items.why: Ringing and muffled hearing are signs that the sound was too much. If they come again and again, the loss may stay.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair noise test in order.
a: Write a guess for each place
Play the same steady sound at the same volume
Hold the phone at the same height and distance
items.why: The guess comes first, so the test can surprise you. Only one thing changes at a time, and each reading is repeated because one try can be a fluke.

items.p: Plants may respond to the vibration of a chewing caterpillar. What do we still not know about plants and our noise?
items.a: Appel and Cocroft found in 2014 that plants responded to vibrations of chewing. Very few studies have looked at what human noise does to plants, so it is an open question.
items.why: A strong answer names the finding and says that almost all noise research has been on people, birds and sea mammals.

items.p: Which is true of the 15 days in India's noise rules?
opts: Loudspeakers may be used all night on them
Crackers have no limit on them
A state may relax night quiet hours to midnight
items.why: A state may allow loudspeakers until midnight on up to 15 days in a year, for festivals. The rest of the rules still apply.

items.p: Which is the odd one out: smoke alarm, train horn, ambulance siren, ticking clock?
items.a: The ticking clock, because it is not made to warn.
items.why: The others are made loud on purpose, to stand out and to carry a meaning that people have learned.

items.p: Draw two opposite waves and the line they make when added together.
items.a: One wave that rises and falls, another that falls where the first rises, and a flat line for their sum.
items.why: Noise-cancelling headphones play the opposite of the incoming sound, so that squeezing and stretching of the air add to nothing.

items.p: Noise limits are set for human ears and measured where people live.

views.who: Campaigners such as the Awaaz Foundation
views.says: The limits protect health, so they should apply equally to every source and every maker of the sound.

views.who: Biologists who study animals in cities (an imagined view)
views.says: Other beings hear different pitches, and a rule shaped to human ears leaves out what birds, dogs and whales need.

items.ask: Should a rule about noise count what a bird or a dog hears?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says that the human limits are a start. Animals could be added by measuring the pitches they hear and the places they live. This is not done yet.
items.why: Both views are real. Neither is wrong, and the first has been the way rules have been written so far.

items.p: A chicken's ear can grow new hair cells after loud sound, and a person's ear cannot.
items.why: True. Researchers found this in birds in 1987 and 1988. Why mammals cannot is still being worked out.

items.p: A sound with 100 times the energy of another is ____ decibels higher.
items.why: Every factor of 10 in energy is 10 decibels. 100 is 10 × 10, so it is 20 decibels.

items.p: Why can a silent electric scooter be a danger?
opts: People who cannot see it rely on hearing it
It runs slower than other scooters
items.why: People who are blind, and anyone stepping off a kerb, use hearing to know a vehicle is near. The European Union has required new electric cars to make a sound at low speeds since 2019.

worksheets.title: Reasoning with decibels and evidence (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to reason about energy, evidence and fair rules, and to argue both sides of questions that scientists and neighbours still disagree about.

items.p: A cracker reads 125 decibels at 4 metres. In the open, how many decibels would it read at 2 metres?
items.why: Halving the distance adds about 6 decibels, so 125 + 6 = 131. At 1 metre it would be close to 137.

items.p: A road reads 70 decibels. Half of the cars are taken off. What is the new level?
items.why: Half the sources takes off only about 3 decibels. The lower numbers come only when most of the cars are gone.

items.p: A sound too quiet to hurt the ear cannot harm health, even if it goes on night after night.
items.why: False. In 2018 the World Health Organization found strong evidence that long-lasting road noise at night raises the risk of heart disease. This happens at levels far below those that damage hearing.

items.p: Cotton wool cuts about 6 decibels. About how many times less sound energy reaches the ear?
items.why: 3 decibels is half the energy and 6 decibels is half again, so about one quarter, which is 4 times less.

items.p: A foam earplug cuts about 25 decibels. About how many times less energy reaches the ear?
items.why: Every 10 decibels is 10 times less, so 20 decibels is 100 times less and 5 more decibels is about 3 times again. That makes close to 300.

items.p: Scientists still disagree about hidden hearing loss in people. What evidence would you try to collect to settle it?
items.a: A test that can see the links between hair cells and nerve in living people. Or a large study of young people with a lot of noise in their past and with little, using careful tests of hearing speech in noise.
items.why: A strong answer says that the evidence in mice is clear, and that people need a test that can detect what a normal test misses.

items.p: Sort each statement by whether India's noise rules contain it.
cats: It is not in the rules
items: Loudspeakers need written permission
It is in the rules
A night-shift worker has quiet hours by day
It is not in the rules
A silence zone is within 100 metres of a hospital, school or court
It is in the rules
The limits take account of what dogs and birds hear
It is not in the rules
Limits are given in dB(A)
It is in the rules
items.why: The rules set limits for areas and times and set conditions for loudspeakers. They do not cover shift workers by day or the hearing of other animals, which is part of the debate about whose sound counts.

items.p: Which result best shows that noise, and not something else, slowed the reading of children beside a railway?
opts: The lag ended when the noise was cut
items.why: If removing the noise removes the lag, noise was the cause. A single school or a teacher's opinion cannot rule out other causes.

items.p: A friend says, 'I am used to the trains, so they cannot harm me.' Give two reasons this is wrong.
items.a: Hair cells may be lost, which makes the noise seem less. Also the body's stress response and the heart rate during sleep still respond to each train, though you may not wake.
items.why: A good answer gives the hair-cell reason and the sleeping-body reason.

items.p: A festival loudspeaker plays until midnight on the last night.

views.says: This is one of the few nights a year when the community celebrates together, and the state allows it.

views.who: A mother whose baby is ill (an imagined view)
views.says: A baby cannot move away from the sound or sleep through the noise, and the quiet hours protect those who are already weak.

items.ask: What would you try before banning it or allowing it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer looks for a middle way, such as turning the speakers away from homes, lowering the volume, ending earlier or moving the stage.
items.why: Both are real. The rules allow a few relaxed days, and the child's health and the community's joy are both worth protecting.

items.p: A hospital ward has many alarms, and most do not need action. What is the best fix?
opts: Rank alarms so only the urgent ones sound loudly
items.why: A warning that sounds too often is ignored. Ranking keeps the urgent ones rare enough to be believed.

items.p: A classroom reads 78 decibels by day. A silence zone's limit by day is 50. The gap is ____ decibels.
items.why: 78 − 50 = 28. That is a very big gap, since every 10 decibels is 10 times the energy.

items.p: Match each warning to what it tells us.
pairs: The steam has reached full pressure
A cyclone or a tsunami is coming
items.why: A warning works because people have learned what it means. A sound with no agreed meaning warns nobody.

items.p: The sound of your own heartbeat in a quiet room: is it noise? Argue it in two sentences for each side.
items.a: Noise: it is unwanted when you are trying to sleep. Not noise: it is your own body and a sign of life, and you did not choose to hear it but it is yours.
items.why: A strong answer sees that noise is about the listener, and a meter would give a single number for both views.

items.p: Plants have no ears, so noise and vibration cannot matter to them.
items.why: False. In 2014 Appel and Cocroft showed that plants made more defence chemicals when played the vibrations of a caterpillar chewing. They sense vibration through their leaves.

quiz.p: Two neighbours hear the same drumbeat. One calls it music and the other calls it noise. What does this show?
opts: Music is always quieter than noise
quiz.why: A meter reads the same for both, so the difference is in the listeners. Noise is a judgement, which is why people disagree about it.

quiz.p: One auto horn reads 90 decibels at your window. About what do two such horns read together?
quiz.why: Twice the sound energy adds about 3 decibels. Choosing 180 adds the numbers like ordinary numbers, which decibels do not do.

quiz.p: A phone reads 80 decibels at 1 metre from a steady sound in the open. About what at 4 metres?
quiz.why: 4 metres is two doublings of distance, and each takes off about 6 decibels, so 80 − 12 = 68.

quiz.p: Why does hearing lost to loud sound not come back in people?
opts: The nerve to the brain is cut
Hair cells that die are not replaced
quiz.why: Humans are born with all the hair cells they will ever have. Birds and fishes can grow new ones, and people cannot.

quiz.p: A cracker bang can harm the ear even though the ear has a guard muscle. Why?
opts: The guard works only when asleep
The muscle needs a tenth of a second, and the bang is quicker
quiz.why: The acoustic reflex takes about a tenth of a second to tighten. A bang reaches full strength in less than a thousandth of a second.

quiz.p: After a loud wedding your hearing returns by morning. What may still be true?
opts: Some links to the hearing nerve may be lost
All the hair cells have grown back
The ear's guard has been mended
quiz.why: In mice, loud sound can destroy up to half of the nerve links while hearing tests pass. Whether this happens in people is still debated.

quiz.p: A lorry passes at night and you sleep on. Is your body affected?
opts: No, nothing happens unless you wake
Only if the lorry is very loud
Yes, heartbeat and blood pressure can rise
quiz.why: Hearing never switches off in sleep. The body can react to each passing noise, and years of this are linked with heart disease.

quiz.p: Great tits sing at a higher pitch in noisy cities. Why does that help?
opts: Traffic rumble is low, so a higher song is heard above it
quiz.why: Low rumble covers low songs. A higher song sits above the rumble and carries better.

quiz.p: In India's 2000 noise rules, loudspeakers may not be used in the open when?
opts: At any time of the day
Between 10 at night and 6 in the morning, unless allowed
quiz.why: The quiet hours are 10 at night to 6 in the morning. A state may relax them to midnight on up to 15 days in a year.

quiz.p: A cracker reads 120 decibels at 4 metres. A child fires it at 1 metre. What level reaches the child?
quiz.why: Each halving of distance adds about 6 decibels, and 4 metres to 1 metre is two halvings. So the child gets about 12 more.

quiz.p: Which best protects your ears at a loud function?
opts: Foam earplugs and sitting far from the speakers
Sitting beside the speaker and enjoying it
quiz.why: Cotton wool cuts only 5 to 7 decibels. Earplugs cut 15 to 30, and distance cuts it more. Close to the speaker the sound is strongest, and enjoying it does not protect hair cells.

quiz.p: With earphones, which of the three levers are left to you?
quiz.why: The earphone sits inside the ear, so there is no distance or barrier. Volume and hours are what you can change.

quiz.p: A child's weekly allowance is 40 hours at 75 decibels. What is the safe time at 84 decibels?
quiz.why: 84 is 9 decibels above 75, which is three steps of 3. The time halves three times: 40 → 20 → 10 → 5.

quiz.p: What makes a warning sound work?
opts: It stands out, can be located and has a meaning people have learned
It is the highest pitch possible
It lasts as long as it can
quiz.why: A warning is noticed because it stands out, found because it can be located, and acted on because people know what it means.

quiz.p: A hospital ward's machines beep all shift, and most beeps need no action. Why is that a danger?
opts: Staff may stop responding, even to real alarms
quiz.why: A warning that sounds too often is tuned out. That is alarm fatigue.

warmup.q: A whisper is about 30 decibels and talking about 60. About how many times more sound energy does talking carry?
What does the A in dB(A) mean?
warmup.a: The meter counts each pitch about as strongly as a human ear hears it.
They turn the movement of liquid in the cochlea into nerve signals.

warmup.q: Can a person's ear grow new hair cells?
warmup.a: No. Birds, fishes and frogs can, but people and other mammals cannot.

warmup.q: How many decibels louder are two equal sounds than one?
Name the three levers for protecting the ear.
warmup.a: The source, the path (distance or a barrier) and the time.

warmup.q: In India's rules, between which hours may loudspeakers not be used in the open?
warmup.a: Between 10 at night and 6 in the morning, unless the state allows it for a festival.

warmup.q: Name three things that make a warning work.
warmup.a: It stands out, it can be found, and it has a meaning that people have learned.

ask_kids: What is the loudest sound you heard today, and what is the sound you most wanted to hear? Were they the same?
Where in your home or street would you put a quiet corner, and what would you change to make it quieter?
When you use earphones, how loud are they, and how long? What would you check after this lesson?
Which sound at a festival do you love, and who nearby might not love it? What could make it better for both?
Why do you think a siren goes up and down instead of staying on one note?
If you could ask a bird or a street dog what they think of our noise, what do you think they would say?

jokes.j: What did the hair cell say to the loud wedding band?
jokes.a: 'Please turn it down. I am already bent out of shape.'

jokes.j: What did one ear say to the other ear?
jokes.a: 'Between us, we have a lot of sound ideas.'

jokes.j: Knock, knock. Who is there? Decibel. Decibel who?
jokes.a: 'Decibel is not working, so I had to knock!'

jokes.j: Why did the teacher in the school beside the railway keep getting derailed?
jokes.a: A train came through her lesson every four and a half minutes.

jokes.j: What did the pressure cooker say to the stove?
jokes.a: 'Stop turning up the heat or I will blow my whistle on you!'

jokes.j: Why did the drum never win an argument?
Why did the decibel go to school?
jokes.a: To get a higher level of education.

jokes.j: Why did the bird sing higher in the city?
jokes.a: The traffic was already doing the low notes.

jokes.j: Why did the mixer-grinder lose the whispering contest?
jokes.a: It only has two settings: grind and GRIND.

spotted.text: In your kitchen, switch on the mixer-grinder or listen to the pressure cooker's whistle from the next room. Notice how much louder it sounds at arm's length than from two rooms away, and how a closed door changes it.
spotted.art: A kitchen with a mixer-grinder running and sound lines getting thinner towards a far room.

spotted.text: On the bus or in an auto, notice how often horns blow and what they were for. Count the horns in one minute and ask how many told anybody something they did not already know.
spotted.art: A child on a bus seat counting horn blasts on her fingers.

spotted.text: Look for a 'No Horn' or 'Silence Zone' board near a hospital or school on your way. Notice if the horns stop, and how far from the board the quiet starts.
spotted.art: A road sign with a crossed-out horn beside a hospital gate.

spotted.text: At a festival or a wedding, notice where the loudspeakers are and where the guests stand. Notice who sits near the speakers, and who sits at the back, and which babies and older relatives have been taken outside.
spotted.art: A hall with large loudspeakers on stage and chairs filling up from the back.

spotted.text: On a bus or train, watch someone's earphones. Notice if you can hear their music from the next seat. If you can, it is a sign the volume is too high.
spotted.art: A child looking at a passenger with earphones that leak small sound lines.

spotted.text: Listen to the birds at dawn and again at the busiest time of day. Notice whether the song is the same, and whether the birds sing before the traffic starts.
spotted.art: A crow, a koel and a magpie-robin on a wire with a quiet road below at dawn.

spotted.text: Watch a street dog or a pet on a night with crackers. Notice where the animal goes to hide and what she or he does, and how long it takes to settle afterwards.
spotted.art: A dog under a cot with her ears flat while distant flashes light the window.

spotted.text: Listen for the pressure cooker's whistle, a train's horn and an ambulance siren on a normal day. Notice that each one makes you do something without a word being said.
spotted.art: A kitchen, a railway crossing and an ambulance, each with its own sound pattern.

applications: Workers who use road drills, looms or grinders wear ear muffs or foam earplugs. Look for them at a building site, or ask a relative who works in a loud place. Notice what they use and how well it fits.

The silencer on an auto or a scooter is a metal box on the exhaust. Inside, the gas passes through chambers and holes, and the sound bounces around and loses energy. Look under a parked scooter to find it.

Phones and earphones now warn you when you listen too loud for too long. This follows a global standard for safe listening devices set by the World Health Organization and the International Telecommunication Union in 2019. Find the setting on a phone with a grown-up.
Many hospitals and some schools have silence-zone boards on the road outside. They apply the rule that sets lower limits within 100 metres. Look for one, and notice whether the traffic obeys it.
Cities draw noise maps by measuring many places and times, and use them to decide where to put barriers and where to reroute a road. Your noise map of home and street is a small one.

Hearing aids and cochlear implants help people whose hair cells cannot do their work. One makes the sound louder, and the other goes round the damaged cells. Many Deaf people use sign language, with or without either.
Tall solid panels stand beside some flyovers, railway lines and metro viaducts to lower the sound reaching homes. Look for them, and notice which side of the panel is quieter.

In some coastal villages, sirens on towers warn of cyclones and tsunamis. Alerts from India's tsunami warning centre reach the coastal authorities, who can set them off. Each siren is made loud and made to carry far, because a warning has to reach everyone.

maths.problem: One auto horn measures 90 decibels at your window. Every doubling of the number of horns adds about 3 decibels, and every ten times as many horns adds 10. Find the level for 2 horns, 10 horns and 100 horns. A friend says 2 horns make 180. Say what is wrong.
maths.answer: 2 horns: about 93. 10 horns: 100. 100 horns: 110. The friend added the numbers, but decibels count how many times the energy has grown.
maths.explain: Two horns carry 2 times the energy, so 90 + 3 = 93. Ten horns carry 10 times the energy, so 90 + 10 = 100. A hundred carry 100 times, so 90 + 20 = 110. Energy adds. Decibels count the tens of times it has grown, so they do not add like ordinary numbers.
maths.context: This problem uses a horn at your window to show how decibels combine when sources are added.
maths.why_maths: The decibel scale counts multiplications of energy. Reading it correctly needs this ratio sum, or a street of horns would seem twice as loud as it is.

maths.problem: A mixer-grinder reads 90 decibels and ordinary talk reads 60. How many times more sound energy does the mixer-grinder carry? What roughly 104 decibels against 74?
maths.explain: Both gaps are 30 decibels. Each 10 decibels is 10 times the energy, so 30 decibels is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000. The same gap gives the same ratio wherever the two numbers sit on the scale.
maths.context: This problem asks how much more energy a loud sound carries than a quiet one.
maths.why_maths: The decibel scale is a ratio scale. A gap of the same size means the same multiplying factor, which is why one number can describe sounds from a whisper to a cracker.

maths.problem: A steady source reads 100 decibels at 1 metre in the open. Each doubling of distance takes off about 6 decibels. Find the level at 2, 4, 8 and 16 metres. At about what distance does it fall to 64 decibels?
maths.answer: 94, 88, 82 and 76 decibels. It falls to 64 at 64 metres.
maths.explain: Each doubling takes off 6: 100 → 94 → 88 → 82 → 76. To reach 64 we must take off 36, which is 6 doublings. Doubling 6 times from 1 metre gives 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 64 metres.
maths.context: This problem uses the distance pattern from the third part of the noise map, with a louder source.
maths.why_maths: Distance makes sound fall in a repeating pattern, a fixed drop for each doubling. Spotting a pattern like this predicts a reading you never measured.

maths.problem: A child's safe weekly listening is 40 hours at 75 decibels, and every 3 decibels more halves the time. Fill in the safe hours for 75, 78, 81, 84, 87 and 90 decibels. Then say how long is safe at 100 decibels, which many phones can reach at full volume.
maths.answer: 40, 20, 10, 5, 2.5 and 1.25 hours. At 100 decibels, only about 7 minutes in a week.
maths.explain: Each step of 3 halves the time. From 75 to 100 is 25 decibels, about 8 steps of 3 and a bit more. Halving 8 times gives 40 ÷ 256, about 0.16 hours. The extra third of a step makes it about 0.12 hours, or about 7 minutes.
maths.context: This problem works out the weekly allowance for earphones at several volumes.
maths.why_maths: Repeated halving shows how quickly safe time collapses as the volume rises. A graph of the hours bends sharply, which is the reason the allowance is given as a pair of numbers.

maths.problem: A foam earplug cuts 25 decibels and cotton wool cuts 6 decibels. About how many times less sound energy does each let through? How many times better is the earplug?
maths.answer: Earplug roughly 300 times less. Cotton wool about 4 times less. The earplug is about 80 times better.
maths.explain: 6 decibels is two halvings of the energy, which is 4 times less. 25 decibels is 20 decibels, which is 100 times, and 5 more, which is about 3 times, so roughly 300 times. 300 ÷ 4 is about 75, so about 80 times better.
maths.context: This problem compares two ways of protecting the ear using the energy ratio of each cut.
maths.why_maths: A difference of a few decibels sounds small, but the ratio of energies is large. This sum shows why cotton wool gives so little protection.

maths.problem: A class of 40 children talking reads 80 decibels. Each time you halve the number of equal talkers, about 3 decibels come off. Find the level for 20, 10, 5 and 1 children. Why does one child alone not read 40?
maths.answer: 77, 74, 71 and about 64 decibels. One child carries one fortieth of the energy, which is only about 16 decibels less, not 40.
maths.explain: Halving 40 children to 20 gives 77, halving to 10 gives 74, and halving to 5 gives 71. From 40 children to 1 child is about 5.3 halvings, so 80 − 16 = 64, close to the 60 of ordinary talk. A level of 40 would be 40 decibels below 80, which is only one ten-thousandth of the energy. One child is one fortieth of it.
maths.context: This problem asks why removing talkers from a class only lowers the level a little.
maths.why_maths: Taking away half of the sources gives a fixed drop, not half the number. This is why very large cuts in traffic are needed to make a street feel much quieter.
